summary: For ages 10–11 (UK KS2 Year 6 Electricity): children compare series circuits and give REASONS for variations in how components behave — brightness of bulbs, loudness of buzzers, and the on/off effect of switch positions. The core objective is explanation, not just observation: moving beyond 'more cells = brighter' to reasoning about why adding more bulbs in series dims each one, why a switch position breaks or completes the loop, and why a buzzer is louder with more cells. Work is driven by systematic one-change-at-a-time comparison and kept qualitative (series circuits for the main investigations, with parallel only as an optional extension prediction; no Ohm's law or quantitative resistance). The central misconception to confront is 'current used up on the way round' — the idea that the bulb nearest the battery is brightest. In a series loop the current is the same everywhere, so identical series bulbs glow equally (apart from small differences between real bulbs).
misconceptions: Current used up / attenuation — the bulb nearest the battery is brightest and later ones dimmer; in series all bulbs are EQUALLY bright.
Confusing adding components with adding cells — expecting 'more bulbs = brighter' when more bulbs in series makes each dimmer.
Clashing currents — explaining brightness by current meeting from both terminals.
Thinking a component's behaviour depends on its POSITION in the series loop rather than on the whole circuit.
Treating 'energy is shared/used up' too literally — useful as a KS2 reason for dimming but must not harden into 'current gets used up' (KS3 corrects this with resistance/current).

activities.title: Compare-and-reason circuit bench: add a second bulb
steps: Build or set up a series circuit with one bright bulb and one cell; observe and name its brightness.
Add a SECOND identical bulb in series. Before looking, predict whether the first bulb will stay the same, get brighter, or get dimmer, and whether the two bulbs will match.

Observe that BOTH bulbs are dimmer than the single bulb was and that the two identical bulbs glow equally (any small difference comes from the bulbs themselves, not from which one is nearer the cell).

Trace the current all the way round the loop (use a simulation's current indicator/band, or ammeters placed at different points in a real circuit) and check that it is the same through both bulbs; drawn arrows show the path but cannot measure the current.
State a reason using a sentence frame: 'This bulb is ___ because ___' (e.g. 'both bulbs are equally dim because the same current flows through both and the cell's push is shared between them').
Reverse the cell and observe that it still makes no difference which bulb is 'first'.
activities.insight: In a single series loop the current is the same through every component, so neither bulb gets 'more' first; adding a second identical bulb dims BOTH equally because the cell's push (voltage) is shared, not because current is used up along the way.

activities.title: Hold the two opposite moves together: more cells vs more bulbs
steps: Starting from a steady single-bulb circuit, add a second CELL in series, facing the same way as the first, and observe the bulb brighten.
Reset, then add a BULB in series and observe each bulb dim.
Use a side-by-side compare view (two circuits shown together) to hold both moves at once.
Sort or explain: which change increases brightness and which decreases it, and WHY — 'more cells push harder; more bulbs in series share the push between more components.'
Open a switch in the loop and observe the whole loop die; explain that an open switch breaks the complete path so nothing flows.
activities.insight: Adding cells and adding bulbs are opposite moves with different causes: more cells (in series) increase the push so bulbs brighten; more bulbs in series share the push so each dims. A switch simply completes or breaks the loop.

activities.title: Explain-it-back: challenge the reason and give evidence
steps: After a comparison, state out loud or in writing why the observed change happened.
Respond to a challenge such as 'your two bulbs are dim — why? are you sure the first isn't brighter?' and defend the answer with evidence from the circuit.

Answer probing extensions: If you unscrew the second bulb in a series pair, what happens to the first — and why? Does swapping the order (bulb-then-buzzer vs buzzer-then-bulb) change anything? Why does adding cells brighten but adding series bulbs dim?
Predict the PARALLEL case: two bulbs side by side (in parallel) compared with a single bulb, and say why.
activities.insight: A reasoned explanation must coordinate two ideas — current is the same everywhere in a series loop, while the push (voltage) is shared between components — and this reasoning transfers to buzzers, to unscrewing a bulb, and to new configurations.

checkQuestion: Two identical bulbs are connected one after the other (in series) with a single cell. One child says the bulb nearest the battery will be brighter because it gets the current first. Are the two bulbs equally bright or not — and explain why.
checkAnswer: Both bulbs are equally bright. In a single series loop the current is the same through every component, so neither bulb gets 'more' first. Both are dimmer than a single bulb would be, because the cell's energy (voltage) is now shared between the two bulbs.
